Yes — rebasing a branch you've already pushed is safe **as long as no one else is working from it**, but it does rewrite history, so the key thing is coordinating with anyone who shares the branch.

## What happens

Rebasing a pushed branch rewrites the commits, so their hashes change. When you push afterward, git rejects it with a non-fast-forward error, because the remote history and your local history no longer share the same commits.

## How to push after a rebase

You need a force push:

```
git push --force-with-lease
```

**Prefer `--force-with-lease` over plain `--force`.** It only succeeds if the remote branch is where you last saw it — so if someone else pushed new commits in the meantime, the push fails instead of silently erasing their work. Plain `--force` overwrites unconditionally.

## When it's safe

- **Branches only you use** (personal feature branches, solo work) — go ahead, this is routine.
- **An open pull request that's yours** — generally fine; the PR updates automatically and reviewers see the new history. Just note that any pending review comments may attach to now-outdated commits.

## When to avoid it

- **Shared branches** (`main`, `develop`, or a branch other people have branched off or pulled) — anyone who based work on the old commits will hit merge conflicts and duplicate commits when they pull. If a shared branch must be rewritten, you need to communicate clearly and get everyone to rebase their local copies (`git pull --rebase`).
- **Published releases or tags** — tags point to specific commits; rewriting beneath them causes real problems.

## Alternatives if history is messy

- If you just want to catch up with upstream changes and your history is already pushed, consider `git merge` instead of rebase.
- If you only need to tweak the *last* commit, `git commit --amend` rewrites less history (same force-push caveats apply).

**Rule of thumb:** rebase your own unshared work freely; once a branch has collaborators, rebase only if everyone agrees, and always use `--force-with-lease`.
